utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-00-39-I, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecution is represented by myself, Carla Del Ponte, and by Mr. Nicola Piacente.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. On behalf of the accused, I'm Defence counsel Igor Pantelic, specially for this Initial Appearance, Rule 62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic and Madam Prosecutor, I understand that the transcript is being recorded, although it's not appearing on our screens. Provided there is a transcript, that is a sufficient record of the proceedings. Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Momcilo Krajisnik, born on the 20th of January, 1945, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you hear the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. This is the Initial Appearance of the accused in this case. The hearing is to be conducted in accordance with Rule 62 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and the first matter concerns the indictment and the accused's pleas to it. The accused is charged in an indictment containing nine counts, alleging genocide, crimes against humanity, and breaches of the Geneva Convention. He has the right, Mr. Pantelic, as you know, to have the indictment read out before he pleads to it. That is a right which he may waive. Mr. Pantelic, does your client waive the right or does he want the indictment read out?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was the result of yesterday's and this morning's discussion. In terms of procedural economy and all ongoing trials here and the lack of time for all of us, he's waiving his right to hear the indictment. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The next stage is the accused's pleas to the indictment. The Rules provide that the accused must be informed that, within 30 days of today, he will be called on to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on each count. But should he so request, he may enter his pleas today. So Mr. Pantelic, I have two questions for you: Does the accused understand the indictment and the matters he has to plead to? Secondly, does he wish to enter his pleas today, or are you asking for an adjournment to consider the matter further?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Prior to answering your question, please allow me to bring to your attention, I would say, such kind of technical, procedural matters which might be of significance, maybe of less significance, importance, to the issue of the proceedings according to Rule 62. Briefly, yesterday I was conferring with my client and he was in possession of two copies of the original, genuine indictment and the amended indictment. It was quite strange to see that these two documents are with the same dates; namely, with the 21st of March. When I was in contact with the officials of the Registry, I requested the original indictments in English, the English is authoritative. After a brief review, I saw on page 17 of the original indictment that the last page, signed by my distinguished colleague, Madam Prosecutor Carla Del Ponte, was sent from the court from Arusha. This page is, with the letters and the styles, not in conformity with the other pages of the indictment. What I would like to outline, there is nothing special in these previous proceedings about the amended indictment, in Counts -- Count 9, where, by error or by omission, a reference to Article 7(1) and 7(3) was omitted, so the Defence would not like to argue anymore this issue, because there is no practical relevance to this procedure. However, the Defence is obliged to bring to your attention, Your Honour, the fact that two copies of the indictment in the B/C/S language, which is the mother tongue of my client, are practically the same. So at the first glance, we were a little bit confused because we were in possession of two copies of the indictment; first, the initial indictment and then the amended indictment, and practically the same, with the two same dates, the 21st of March, which is not in accordance with the English version. I would just like to make a record that it is not consistent. As I said, it is nothing substantial, but it is a small error, maybe a typing error, maybe a technical error. In addition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, let me interrupt you. If anything turns on it, it can be looked into in due course. But at the moment, it doesn't seem to be a matter which need hold the Court up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was my idea, just to bring to the attention of Your Honour these facts. About the further proceedings, I believe that Mr. Krajisnik will enter a plea today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, will you stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've heard what your counsel said, that you understand the indictment, the matters you have to plea to, and you are prepared to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on those counts today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. But I would like to ask Your Honours for just one minute, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At this stage, Mr. Krajisnik, we are purely dealing with your pleas to the indictment, and you will be expected to answer guilty or not guilty to each count. Now, unless there's something about that that you want to raise, I propose to put the indictment to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to request from the Trial Chamber to allow me a couple of minutes at this hearing to say a few words in my defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, as I said, at this stage we're dealing with the indictment and your pleas to it. I'll consider any other matters after that has been dealt with, after we have dealt with the other procedural matters. Now, at this stage, I'm going to put the various counts to you. Confine your answers to "guilty" or "not guilty" on each count. You are charged in an indictment, as I said, with nine counts. Counts 1 to 6 allege offences against Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, committed between the 1st of July, 1991 and the 31st of December, 1992. Count 1: Genocide, punishable under Articles 4(3)(a), and 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. To that count, how do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 2 charges you with complicity in genocide, punishable under Articles 4(3)(e), and 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 3 charges extermination, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(b), and 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 4 charges murder, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(a), and 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 5 alleges murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war, as recognised by Common Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Articles 3, and 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 6 charges wilful killing, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Articles 2(a), and 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 7 charges you with persecution during the same period. Count 7: Persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(h), and 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Counts 8 and 9 charge you with deportation and inhumane acts during the same period. Count 8: Deportation, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(d), and 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 9: Inhumane acts (forced transfer), a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(i), and 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Those pleas will be recorded. If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will move to the next stage of the proceedings concerning disclosure and any other procedural matters which may be relevant. Madam Prosecutor, as you know, the Prosecution are required, within 30 days of today, to provide the Defence with copies of the supporting material for the confirmation in a language which the accused understands. May I take it that that matter is in hand?

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, that is correct. I can say that we are ready for the disclosure; that is, all the documents are at the disposal of the Defence. We have some documents that are already at the disposal of the Defence but whose translation has still not been completed into the language of the accused. But this will be done in the next few days. And I would suggest, Mr. President, that the Defence can, already today, gain possession of all the documents, and we will provide the translation of the few other documents that remain in the next week or so. Furthermore, we have 80 statements of witnesses that haven't yet been translated. That will be done within the time limit envisaged by the Rules, and even before that I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. As for the points which Mr. Pantelic was making about the indictment, no doubt you can look into them, and if there is any problem arising you can bring it to the attention of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, indeed. I understood what the Defence counsel said. There is an indictment that I signed. The fact that I signed it in Arusha is simply due to the fact that I am Prosecutor of both Tribunals and sometimes I happen to be there. And I don't think that this has any effect regarding the formal validity of the document. As regards the amended indictment, Mr. President, Defence counsel is quite right, it is the same indictment except that there was a typing errata or an omission made; that is, when the counts were listed, Count 9, Article 7 was omitted, reference to Article 7(1) and 7(3), which you find in all the other documents, and this was probably due to a technical error. We thought it would be sufficient to write a letter to the Confirming Judge in order to indicate this omission which arose, and the Confirming Judge decided that it was necessary to draft an amended indictment because, according to this Judge, the form had to be preserved. But the indictment is the same in fact, in terms of the listing of crimes, it was just the fact that the two numbers were unfortunately left out. I see that Defence counsel has made no formal objections but has just drawn the attention of the President of the Chamber to this. Thank you, Mr. President, for giving me the opportunity to express myself on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make it quite clear, regarding the date, they tell me it is the translation section, it is the date of the translation that is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It appears that nothing turns on these matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can have just a second, please. As I said, it is not a question of the date. In the version in the B/C/S language, there are two copies of absolutely the same indictment. Madam Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the other issue, Your Honour -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- these are matters which I have said which can be dealt with in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If anything turns on them, which at the moment it appears that it doesn't, if you have a further point, you can make it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, as far as disclosure is concerned, I draw to your attention, as you know, that all preliminary motions have to be brought within 30 days of Prosecution disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The other issue which is of the utmost importance is the time limit for the preliminary motions. As I said, I'm here today appearing just on a limited basis, I am here just for the Rule 62. It would not be in accordance with the safeguards of the rights of the accused to consider that from today we have this time limit running. In addition, as the Prosecutor said, they are not ready even today to serve all the necessary documents to my client. So I would respectfully suggest to wait a reasonable time; we could discuss that with the Prosecutor. I suppose that within next week, my client will decide upon the issue of his counsel, because as you know I am involved in another case before this Tribunal so I cannot have two cases simultaneously, and then when the Prosecutor would be ready with all the necessary documents, we could officially start this time limit. That would be my suggestion, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Rules, in fact, provide that the motions have to be with the Tribunal after Prosecution disclosure, and time limits are then set. If there is any difficulty about the time limits, then it's a matter for the Court to consider. But you can tell those who appear for your client that the time limits will, of course, apply and any variation will require an application on their part. But at the moment the time limits run from Prosecution disclosure, not before. Now, that, in fact, deals with all the matters, apart from the order which I have to make. Madam Prosecutor, is there anything which you wish to raise, apart from the matters you've dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic, are there any matters which you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, at this stage. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, your client indicated that he wished to make a statement. No statements can be made at this stage of the proceeding. He can, of course, make his defence when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, as I suggested. But he has his right to pronounce himself. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. There was one final matter, in fact, which I ought to mention to the parties, and that is a date for the next hearing. The Rules require a hearing within 90 days. That, I think, would be a date in July. I'll be informed, if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next stage will be a Status Conference, which has, in fact, to take place within 120 days, not 90. That will bring us to the 26th of July. The order I'll make today is that this matter is adjourned for a Status Conference on the 26th of July, unless the pre-trial Judge -- after the appointment of a pre-trial Judge -- unless the pre-trial Judge orders an earlier conference. So the matter will be adjourned until the 26th of July or earlier order. There will be an order for the detention of the accused in the United Nations Detention Unit. This hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: adjourned at 10.30 a.m.
